title: Proper time along a straight worldline
promptMarkdown:
A clock moves with constant velocity $v$ along the $x$-axis of an inertial laboratory frame and ticks at two events $A$ and $B$.

1. Starting only from the invariance of the interval, derive the relation between the proper time $\tau$ read by the clock between $A$ and $B$ and the laboratory time $\Delta t$ between them. Carry the units.
2. Expand your result for $v\ll c$ to first non-trivial order and evaluate the fractional correction for a jet aircraft at $v = 250\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and for a satellite at $v = 7.7\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
3. At what speed does the clock accumulate exactly half the laboratory time? Give the exact value as a fraction of $c$ and a three-figure decimal.
4. Prove that $\tau\le\Delta t$ for every $v$ with equality only for $v = 0$, and explain in one sentence what would go wrong in the derivation if $v > c$.
hintLadder: In the laboratory the clock's spatial displacement between the ticks is $\Delta x = v\Delta t$. In the clock's own frame, what is its spatial displacement?
Write the interval in both frames and equate.

deterministicChecks.description: the speed at which τ = Δt/2 is 0.866 c

criteria.criterion: τ = Δt√(1 − v²/c²) derived from −c²τ² = −c²Δt² + v²Δt² with the clock's zero displacement in its own frame stated; units checked.
τ ≈ Δt(1 − v²/2c²); fractional corrections ≈ 3.5 × 10⁻¹³ for 250 m/s and ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ for 7.7 km/s.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Expansion and both numbers (to one figure).

criteria.criterion: τ ≤ Δt since 0 ≤ 1 − v²/c² ≤ 1 with equality iff v = 0; for v > c the square root is imaginary — no clock can move faster than light, equivalently the events would be spacelike and no clock could be present at both.

checkExamples.label: correct LaTeX derivation
checkExamples.text: In the lab $\Delta x = v\Delta t$; in the clock frame $\Delta x' = 0$. Invariance gives $-c^2\tau^2 = -c^2\Delta t^2 + v^2\Delta t^2$, so $\tau = \Delta t\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$. Setting $\tau = \Delta t/2$ gives $v = (\sqrt3/2)c \approx 0.866c$.

checkExamples.label: plain-text derivation with gamma
checkExamples.text: tau = dt/γ where γ = 1/sqrt(1-(v/c)^2); half the time needs γ = 2, i.e. v = 0.8660 c.

checkExamples.label: no formula
checkExamples.text: The clock reads less time than the laboratory but I could not derive the factor.
